name: routing-slip
intent: Attach the ordered list of processing steps a message must pass through to the message itself, so its route is decided per message by data the message carries instead of by a centrally configured flow, and each step only has to forward the message to the next entry on its slip.
problem: A message must traverse a sequence of processing steps whose length and order are not known at design-time and differ per message - one purchase order needs a credit-card validation, another one sent over a VPN does not. Neither extreme works: hard-coding the sequence in every component turns each flow change into a deployment of all components, while a central router must know the whole topology and becomes the component every step has to be registered with.
context: Message-oriented integration, ESB or workflow code where a planner can compute the route for a message before the flow starts, where the steps are heterogeneous (different services, teams or transports) and must stay reusable across flows, and where the flow should run without a central orchestrator holding its state - typically long-running, multi-service processes that may be eventually consistent.
benefits: Decentralised routing: no component holds the flow's state, so there is no orchestrator to scale, redeploy or lose - each step reads the slip and forwards the message.
Per-message routes: adding a customer-specific validation, an extra enrichment or a new approval step is a change in the planner's data, not in any existing step.
Steps stay ignorant of their successors, so a step can serve several flows and its owners do not have to know who runs next.
Routing decisions can use anything the planner knows (message type, customer, region, contract) and may differ for every single message, which a static pipeline topology cannot express.
Progress travels with the message (a cursor or the remaining entries), so an operator, a retry or an audit can see how far the flow got and resume from there.
Works across heterogeneous transports: the slip names logical steps and each slip-aware router resolves them, so one flow can pass through queues, HTTP endpoints and local calls.
Combines naturally with compensation: a step can record undo data next to its entry, which yields a loosely coupled transaction across services.
tradeoffs: The flow has no single home: no component can answer "where does this message go next", so understanding and debugging a flow means reconstructing it from many planners and messages - message history or a wire tap becomes mandatory.

The slip is data that directs processing, so a forged or corrupted itinerary can aim a message at components the sender was never meant to reach; allowed step ids or destination schemes must be validated and whitelisted instead of trusted.

Step names or endpoint URIs become a wire contract: in-flight messages produced by an older planner can reference steps that were renamed or removed, and every consumer of the slip must keep their meaning stable.
Itineraries live in message headers, which brokers bound in size; long slips cost bandwidth on every hop and eventually force the itinerary into a claim check or message store.

The model is linear: branching, parallel fan-out or a next step that depends on an intermediate result cannot be expressed honestly - that is Process Manager (central state) or Dynamic Router (recomputed per hop) territory.

Failing mid-slip leaves partial side effects, because the pattern provides no atomicity: steps must be idempotent and either retryable or compensatable, and a lost message simply ends the flow unless something watches for stalled slips.
Late binding couples the slip producer to the routing namespace (queue names, step ids), so topology changes leak into business code that only wanted to describe a process.

participants.responsibility: Computes the ordered list of steps required for one message from message type, content or configuration, attaches it to the message and sends the message to the first entry.
The ordered itinerary as it travels with the message, together with whatever progress marker the implementation keeps (a cursor, a slip index, or only the remaining entries).

Wrapped around each step or embedded in the dispatcher; after the step returns it reads the slip, advances the progress marker and routes the message to the next entry - the only participant that knows the routing mechanics.

Performs one unit of work on the message (validation, enrichment, reservation, notification) and knows nothing about its successor; must be idempotent because delivery along the slip is not transactional.
Carries the message from one step to the next; a slip whose entries live on different transports is still one logical flow.
Optional participant that records per-step undo data for completed steps so that a later failure can roll the flow back instead of leaving half-finished business effects.

use_cases: Order fulfilment where the required steps differ per order and per customer contract: fraud check, address validation, stock reservation, payment, shipping.
Document and claim processing where the route depends on document type, amount or jurisdiction and new steps are added continuously without touching existing handlers.
Message-based integration across several services and transports where the flow must keep running without a central orchestration engine: every service forwards the message together with its slip.
Request-processing middleware in a single process (upload pipeline: virus scan, resize, thumbnail, persist) where the stage list is data of the request and must be visible to operations.
Distributed transactions with compensation: reserve, charge and ship steps that each register an undo action, so a late failure releases the reservation instead of stranding it.
Per-tenant data pipelines where each tenant's contract dictates a different sequence of transformations over the same message.

Apache Camel's Routing Slip EIP carries a per-message, precomputed list of endpoint URIs in the exchange and routes the message through them in order, useful for integration pipelines assembled from reusable endpoints.

Spring Integration's routing-slip header selects the next output channel for each reply, allowing a message to traverse a channel sequence that varies by message; use a named serializable route strategy when the flow crosses process boundaries.

MassTransit's Courier routing slips build an itinerary of activities with execution and compensation logs, fitting long-running multi-service transactions where completed activities may need compensating actions.
avoid_when: The sequence is the same for every message and known at design-time: a static chain (Pipes and Filters, a middleware stack, plain method calls) is simpler and far easier to observe.
The next step depends on intermediate results, or steps must branch, loop or run in parallel: use Process Manager for central state or Dynamic Router to recompute the next hop per message.
One component only has to pick among a handful of destinations from payload content: Content-Based Router or Recipient List is the cheaper, more visible answer.
Producer and consumer share one team and one fixed topology with no per-message variation: the header contract and its versioning cost more than a direct call.
The workflow needs durable state, timeouts and human tasks with visibility: a workflow engine (Process Manager) holds that state, and a slip cannot compensate for its absence.
The itinerary would exceed header limits of the transport or must stay hidden from intermediaries: keep the route central or store it externally behind a claim check.
anti_patterns: Serialising a constant, never-varying step list into every message: a static pipeline is dressed up as data routing and pays header plus contract costs for no flexibility.
Letting a processing step append arbitrary destinations to its own slip: a self-modifying itinerary turns untrusted input into execution control, which is a Dynamic Router without a policy.
Using routing slips for branching, loops or fan-out that the linear model cannot express, so the flow ends up neither expressible nor observable.
Treating the slip as a transaction: there is no atomicity and no rollback of completed steps, so failures leave half-finished business effects.
Shipping internal endpoint names, credentials or the full topology inside messages that leave the trust boundary, exposing the integration landscape to anyone reading the header.
Appending one entry per historical step until the slip becomes de facto message history and blows the broker's header limits.
design_principles: Information hiding: the itinerary exposes step identities, not routing mechanics, and steps never learn the topology or their successors.
Open/closed: new steps and new flows enter through the planner's data and the step registry, without modifying the steps themselves.
Separation of concerns: route computation (planner), route execution (slip-aware router) and unit of work (step) are distinct responsibilities.
Composition over a monolithic process: a flow is a composed sequence of small, reusable transformations.
Data-driven control must be validated: the flow is data, so it must be checked at the boundary (whitelisted steps, bounded length) rather than trusted.
Failure is a normal path: idempotent steps and explicit compensation replace the transaction the pattern cannot provide.
best_practices: Compute the itinerary once, up front, and keep it in a dedicated, versioned header field whose format and step naming are a documented contract.
Validate the slip before dispatching: whitelist step ids or destination schemes, bound the number of entries, and reject malformed itineraries.
Keep progress in the message - advance a cursor or remove the consumed entry - so retries and restarts resume instead of repeating steps.
Make every step idempotent and register undo data whenever its effect is not naturally reversible.
Resolve step ids through a registry rather than hard-coding physical endpoints, so a moved or renamed component does not invalidate in-flight messages.
Emit a correlation identifier, pair the slip with message history or a wire tap, and monitor for slips that stop advancing, because nothing else tracks the flow.
Keep itineraries short; store large ones in a message store behind a claim check and carry only a reference.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Routing Slip (Message Routing chapter): attach the itinerary to the message, and each step's router reads the slip and forwards the message to the next listed component.
